reviewer_type: AI-assisted claim-level source audit with independent read-only post-edit review; no human expert review is claimed.
title: Utility Monster
scope: Claim-level traceability review of the revised article and matching dataset record. Focus: Nozick’s original utility-monster passage and its stated inference; the article’s hypothetical versus editorial numerical illustration; distinctions among total-utility maximizing and other consequentialist commitments; the later negative-utility variation; and reference alignment. This status records editorial traceability, not the soundness of Nozick’s objection, empirical existence of a utility monster, scholarly consensus, exhaustive literature coverage, or expert review.
summary: Nozick’s primary passage in chapter 3, printed p. 41, directly supports the possibility of a utility monster who gains enormously more utility from others’ sacrifices than they lose, and his qualified claim that utilitarian theory ‘seems to require’ sacrificing everyone to increase total utility. The article now attributes this wording narrowly to Nozick, marks its 10-unit calculation as an original conditional illustration, and limits the resulting recommendation to an unrestricted additive total-utility rule under explicit assumptions. The Stanford Encyclopedia supports distinctions among classic total-utility utilitarianism and other consequentialist approaches. Chappell’s accessible Cambridge abstract distinguishes a later negative-utility variant; the full article was not accessed. The IEP entry supplies rights-based context but does not discuss Nozick’s monster. A read-only post-edit reviewer found no material corrections. The article and dataset reference URL sets match; date_verified is 2026-11-01.

sources.title: Negative Utility Monsters

sources.publication: Utilitas 33(4), December 2021, pp. 417–421; published online 24 May 2021; DOI 10.1017/S0953820821000169.
sources.access_level: Publisher abstract and bibliographic record accessed and read; full article not available in the consulted session.
sources.exact_locations_read: Abstract and publication information: the abstract describes Nozick’s monster as a being more efficient than ordinary people at converting resources into wellbeing and presents a variation whose baseline is massive suffering.
sources.limitations: The abstract supports only the distinction and high-level framing of Chappell’s variation; it does not establish the full article’s reasoning or replies. The article does not make this negative variation part of Nozick’s original positive-gain passage.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Nozick presents the possibility of utility monsters that gain enormously more utility from others’ sacrifices than those others lose, and says utilitarian theory seems to require sacrifice of everyone in order to increase total utility.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Chapter 3, ‘Moral Constraints and the State,’ printed p. 41, paragraph beginning ‘Utilitarian theory is embarrassed by the possibility of utility monsters…’
claim_evidence.finding: The primary passage directly supports the description and the attribution. The article retains Nozick’s modal framing (‘possibility’) and his qualified wording (‘seems to require’) rather than presenting his conclusion as an established consequence of every maximizing theory.
claim_evidence.limitation: Only the relevant passage was read in a hosted reproduction; it establishes what Nozick wrote, not the truth of his criticism.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: added direct citation to chapter 3, p. 41, and narrowed the wording to Nozick’s stated hypothetical and inference.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The 10-unit calculation, with 1 welfare point per unit for an ordinary recipient and 100 for the monster, is an editorial illustration and favors the monster only under comparable, additive values with other effects excluded.
claim_evidence.source_title: Original editorial illustration (not a claim attributed to an external source)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Article §3, paragraph beginning ‘As a separate illustration—not Nozick’s example…’
claim_evidence.finding: No consulted source provides these numerical values. The arithmetic follows from the article’s explicit stipulations, and the revised text labels them as editorial rather than Nozick’s figures or an empirical welfare measure.
claim_evidence.limitation: The illustration does not show that interpersonal utility comparisons are measurable or morally decisive.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: explicitly identified the example as editorial and stated its comparability, additivity, and exclusion assumptions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Nozick’s hypothetical concerns an unrestricted additive total-utility view; its implication does not automatically transfer to every consequentialist approach, including views that incorporate distribution, fairness, or priority to worse-off people.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1 on the distinct commitments composing classic utilitarianism; §3 on distributive, fairness-based, prioritarian, average, and negative-utility approaches.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP explains that total aggregation is one commitment among several and reports consequentialist alternatives that assess distribution or prioritize worse-off people. The article now avoids generalizing Nozick’s challenge to all consequentialist theories.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP provides a scholarly taxonomy, not proof that any proposed alternative succeeds or that Nozick’s objection is decisive.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: limited the illustrated result to an unrestricted additive total-utility rule and stated that other objectives yield different conclusions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Chappell’s ‘negative utility monster’ is a later variation that begins from a condition of massive suffering and is distinct from Nozick’s original positive-gain case.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Publisher abstract and article record for Utilitas 33(4), pp. 417–421.
claim_evidence.finding: The abstract explicitly describes the negative variation as starting from massive suffering and identifies it as a variation on Nozick’s positive-gain monster. The article names this as Chappell’s later discussion and discloses abstract-only access.
claim_evidence.limitation: The full article’s arguments and replies were not read; only the abstract and bibliographic record were consulted.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: separated the negative-utility variation from Nozick’s original and disclosed the source access limit.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The Internet Encyclopedia entry supports context about Nozick’s rights and side-constraints but does not directly establish the utility-monster thought experiment.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2 and §2(a), on Anarchy, State, and Utopia, individual rights, and side-constraints; no utility-monster discussion appears in the retrieved sections.
claim_evidence.finding: The article retains the IEP link only as general Nozick context. The original monster’s wording is attributed to the primary passage, not to the IEP entry.
claim_evidence.limitation: The IEP source does not independently corroborate the utility-monster scenario.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: clarified in §10 that the IEP is contextual and not evidence for the original monster’s wording.

unresolved: Nozick’s complete book was not accessed; this audit covers the relevant printed p. 41 passage.
The full text of Chappell’s article was unavailable; the negative-variant claim is supported only by its publisher abstract and bibliographic record.
The hypothetical utility scale and interpersonal comparability are assumptions, not empirical findings.
